text.content:
Much as they might claim otherwise, anarchs have no real structure, and most gangs function independently, meeting occasionally at raves to exchange war stories and compare notes. They pride themselves on being above the petty social games of the Camarilla or the savage infighting of the Sabbat, where a single scandal can spell the end of a centuries-old Kindred. However, anarchs play games of their own regarding standing within the Movement and the respect of their peers; they just go about it differently. Unlike the sects, an anarch's Reputation is not based on position, rites or generation — even a ghoul can have a Reputation among the anarchs. Rather, revolutionaries gain or lose Reputation by their deeds alone, as judged by their comrades-in-arms.

In practice, some anarchs spend as much time building and defending their Reputations as sect members spend pursuing Status. The more overtly an anarch seeks Reputation, the less chance he has of finding it; conversely, the less outwardly concerned he is with his “rep,” the more likely he is to receive one from his peers. If you abuse your Reputation, you will lose it — but if you can hold on to it, such are legends made of.

Reputation Mechanics

Anarchs use Reputation Traits in all the same ways as Camarilla or Sabbat Status (added to Social Challenges, loaned as a favor, etc.), with the following differences:

  • Other anarchs suffer no penalty for ignoring Reputation in a challenge, save whatever punishment the character with Reputation can levy for the disrespect.
  • Anarch Reputation Traits never apply against Camarilla or Sabbat vampires, just as sect Status never applies against anarchs.
  • Although an anarch with greater Reputation is more likely to be believed in a casual setting, Reputation is not the deciding factor in disciplinary proceedings or criminal accusations — all anarchs are considered equal there.
  • Clan standing or the whims of elders do not determine Reputation; only recognition by one's fellow revolutionaries for what a character has achieved (or failed to achieve) does.

Gaining and Losing Reputation

Temporary Reputation Change

Any time during a session that a majority of the anarch characters present (not necessarily a majority of all anarchs in the game) are gathered, they may call a vote to award or remove temporary Reputation Traits from any anarch present. A character may not gain more temporary Reputation than twice her number of permanent Reputation Traits (including Committed) through this method. On a count of three, everyone with the Committed Trait votes thumbs up (favor), thumbs down (opposed) or a fist (abstain); a simple majority wins. There are no appeals, save calling another vote later — which costs the appealing character one temporary Reputation Trait. Unless otherwise agreed, temporary Reputation shifts from these informal votes last only until the end of the session. Players cannot simply award each other temporary Reputation with no in-character basis; the Storyteller or Gossip should be present to keep the system honest.

Permanent Reputation Change

A permanent change requires a full-fledged anarch gathering, and a character other than the one seeking (or deserving) the change must first propose it. At contentious gatherings the Storyteller may require the speaker spend a temporary Reputation Trait just to get the crowd's attention; a Social Test may be needed against opposition. Barring exceptional circumstances, an anarch may not gain more than one permanent positive Reputation Trait per rave, though she may lose as many positive, or gain as many negative, Traits as her fellow anarchs see fit.

System: A vote is called: on a count of three, each character with Committed votes thumbs up/down/fist as above. Removing an existing positive Trait or assigning a negative Trait requires only a simple majority; awarding a new positive Trait requires a 2/3 majority. If the vote passes, the Trait is awarded immediately and cannot be removed until at least the next gathering, barring evidence of fraud. Ghouls can gain or lose Reputation at a rave too, though they generally must accomplish at least twice as much as a vampire would for the same Trait.

The vote is not anonymous: whether a character was for or against is plainly noticeable to all present, barring Discipline use or a similar talent for masking feelings. A character may spend a level of Subterfuge (or an appropriate concealment power) and cup her voting hand to obscure it from all but the tallier; others must win a standard Social Test (retest Empathy) against her to read her true vote.

Boons and Prestation

Anarchs don't recognize formal “boons” or Camarilla-style prestation, but the underlying concepts — tracking favors owed and owed to you — are far from alien to them. Failure to repay an important favor is a common flashpoint for violence in the Movement. The key difference is style: an anarch reminds a friend of a past favor and asks for an equal display of loyalty in return, rather than formally invoking a “life boon” or “prestation debt.” The meaning is the same; the presentation is deliberately informal.

Reputation Traits

An anarch can generally have up to eight Reputation Traits, subject to Storyteller discretion; cities with more anarchs tend to allow more variation, while a handful of anarchs in a small city is likely limited to fewer Traits. The only way to earn Reputation is to become known for a particular accomplishment or talent — lying about one's deeds to gain Reputation is an invitation to disaster once the truth comes out. Standard Status Traits from the core rules can apply just as easily to anarchs (especially established types like barons or emissaries), and the following are additional Traits specific to the Movement:

  • Advocate, Believer, Champion, Preacher. Degrees of Reputation recognizing how well known an anarch is for teaching independent or sect-aligned vampires the true ideals of the Anarch Revolt, gathering recruits, or defusing tensions born of misunderstanding.
  • Bond/Bond Girl. The anarch is a successful spy within one of the larger sects, whether a simple observer or actively working to undermine it from within.
  • Committed. The vampire has proven her dedication to the ideals of the Anarch Revolt and her loyalty to her fellow anarchs after a suitable probationary period and/or trial by fire. Cannot be removed short of the holder leaving the Movement or being permanently banished for betrayal, chronic incompetence, etc.
  • Hardcore. The anarch has gone above and beyond the call of duty, placing herself directly in harm's way to complete a mission of great importance to the Movement despite superior odds, serious personal objections, grave danger of Final Death, or other overwhelming factors.
  • Loaded, Hook-Up, Connected. The anarch is a trusted source of resources: money and equipment, information, or Influence-based favors, respectively.
  • Marked. Through her actions, the anarch has become the target of a Blood Hunt, War Party, or even the Red List. This may count as a negative Reputation Trait in areas where anarchs are trying to keep a low profile.
  • Soldier, Warrior, Veteran, Lifer. Awarded each time an anarch survives a protracted siege, pitched battle, or similar major tactical undertaking (not just a raid or minor brawl). Additional victories beyond the first simply increase the degree of respect granted.
  • Tested. An anarch who survives a successful planned raid or similar organized minor conflict may receive this Trait — only once, after the first such clash; afterward the anarch is expected to know how to take care of herself.
  • True Believer. The anarch has directly placed himself in harm's way for the sake of spreading the ideals of the Anarch Revolt. Most often given to recruiters and emissaries who risk Final Death to spread the Movement's ideals in actively hostile cities.
  • Visionary. The anarch is known for proposing new and useful ideas for the Cause — a more amicable way to divide hunting grounds, a better method to gather Influence, or a tactical plan that saved the city from a Sabbat invasion.

Storytellers should feel free to define additional Reputation Traits fitting a particular gang, territory, or the Movement as a whole.

Negative Reputation Traits

An anarch may possess up to two negative Reputation Traits at a time. A newly awarded negative Trait displaces the oldest one for game-mechanical purposes, though characters remember what actually happened regardless. A negative Trait is generally removed once its holder twice successfully completes the very task he failed at to earn it, or by publicly and conclusively clearing his name of a false accusation.

  • Burnt Out. Given to anarchs who have shown a distinct lack of enthusiasm for the Cause, or who belittle or downplay the importance of the Anarch Revolt.
  • Casualty. The anarch has become careless in word or deed, placing fellow revolutionaries in direct danger.
  • Cherry. Given to anarchs who exhibit dangerous naiveté about the Movement, their gang's goals, or unlife in general; usually only applied once a vampire's inexperience has caused serious problems or bodily harm to fellow anarchs.
  • Defeated. The anarch recently lost a fair fight or personal duel (not a forced retreat from overwhelming odds).
  • Overzealous. The vampire's refusal to compromise her (often hypocritical, self-important) personal beliefs has needlessly endangered other anarchs or the city as a whole.
  • Thug. The anarch is too eager to start a fight or put himself (and often others) at risk, even when it isn't the best option.
  • Unenlightened. Even after having them explained, the anarch cannot remember essential components of the Anarch Revolt — the history of the Cause, the Convention of Thorns, the principles of the Status Perfectus, etc. Usually awarded after public demonstration of such ignorance, especially in front of sect members.
  • Unreliable. The vampire failed to perform a key duty for his gang that was explicitly his responsibility.
  • Vain (also Cocky, Full of Himself). The vampire claimed mastery of some field and went on to fail publicly, preferably in an impressive or physically dangerous way.

Keeping Reputation in Perspective

Reputation Traits quantify something hazy and subjective in the World of Darkness. A character can ride a victory to the top of the world one night, only to find the backlash from his next failure more intense since others “expected better” of him. A negative Reputation vote doesn't mean the other players have it in for the character out of game — troupes are encouraged to keep that distinction clear. If Reputation starts becoming an out-of-game popularity contest, the troupe (or the Storyteller alone) is free to change the system entirely; rules should always serve the chronicle, not the other way around.
